title: Activity Selection
directAnswer: To pick the most non-overlapping activities, sort them by finish time and greedily take each activity whose start is ≥ the finish of the last one you took. Always choosing the earliest-finishing compatible activity leaves the maximum room for everything after it — an exchange argument proves this is optimal. O(n log n) from the sort, O(n) for the scan.

remember.pattern: Sort by finish time, take earliest-finishing compatible activity
remember.formula:
sort activities by finish time asc
count = 0; lastEnd = -∞
for (s, f) in activities:
    if s >= lastEnd:
        count += 1
        lastEnd = f
return count
rules: Sort by **finish** time, not start time and not duration — finishing earliest is what frees the most future room.
Pick an activity only if its start ≥ the last selected finish; then update lastEnd to that finish.
Decide your overlap convention: if an activity starting exactly when another ends is compatible, use `>=`; if not, use `>`.
Greedy here is provably optimal via an exchange argument — the earliest-finishing choice is never worse than any other first pick.
This is the maximisation twin of 'minimum meeting rooms' and 'non-overlapping intervals to remove'.
whenToUse: Maximise the COUNT of mutually non-overlapping intervals you can keep
Single resource (one room, one CPU) shared by competing time intervals
Each item has a fixed start and finish; you keep or drop it whole
Equivalent: minimum intervals to delete so the rest don't overlap (n − kept)
antiSignals: Activities have weights/profits and you want max total value → that's weighted interval scheduling (DP, not greedy)
You may run multiple resources in parallel → minimum-rooms / sweep-line problem
You can split or preempt an activity → different model entirely
You need the actual partition into rooms, not a single max set → sweep line
remember.takeaway: Sort-by-finish-time is the canonical greedy for interval problems. The earliest-finishing activity is a safe first choice because it dominates: any optimal solution can be rewritten to start with it without losing count. Recognise the same move in Non-overlapping Intervals, Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons, and Maximum Length of Pair Chain.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you sort by FINISH time (not start or duration) and can justify with an exchange argument why the earliest-finishing compatible activity is always a safe greedy choice.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting by start time or by shortest duration — both produce counterexamples — or comparing each new activity against the wrong reference instead of the last selected finish.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Give the exchange-argument proof: take any optimal set, swap its first activity for the globally earliest-finishing one; compatibility is preserved and the count is unchanged, so a solution led by the greedy pick is also optimal.

problemStatement:
You are given `n` activities, each with a start time `start[i]` and a finish time `finish[i]`. A single resource can run only one activity at a time, so two activities are **compatible** only if they don't overlap.

Select the **maximum number** of mutually compatible activities — i.e. the largest subset whose intervals don't overlap. Return that count (and optionally the chosen activities).
constraints: An activity ending exactly when another begins is compatible (boundary touch allowed) — confirm with the interviewer
Times may be large; use long if you sum or subtract them
understanding: All activities compete for one resource over time. We want to cram in as many as possible. The number kept is what matters, not their total length — so a single long activity is worth the same as a short one (one each). The trick is choosing which to keep so that early choices don't needlessly block later ones.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If one activity finishes exactly when another starts, are they compatible?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Usually yes — touching endpoints don't overlap. I'll use start ≥ lastEnd. If the convention is strict, I switch to >.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we maximise the count of activities or some total value/duration?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The count. If activities had weights, this becomes weighted interval scheduling, which needs DP, not greedy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there one resource or several?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One. With multiple resources in parallel it becomes a minimum-rooms / sweep-line problem instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the inputs already sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll assume not and sort by finish time, which is the O(n log n) part. If they're pre-sorted, the scan alone is O(n).

examples.explanation: By finish time, pick (1,2), then (3,4), then (5,7), then (8,9) → 4 activities.
Pick (10,20) then (20,30) — they touch at 20, compatible. (12,25) overlaps both.
All three end at 10 and overlap pairwise; only one fits.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Subset (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to frame the search space, then immediately note it's exponential and motivate the greedy.
hints: We want the largest compatible subset. The most literal idea is to consider every possible subset of activities.
For each of the 2ⁿ subsets, check whether all its activities are pairwise non-overlapping, and track the largest valid one.
Checking a subset for compatibility costs O(n) after sorting it. 2ⁿ subsets makes this exponential — fine to state, impossible to run for n = 30+.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ subsets; validating each (sort or scan for overlaps) costs up to O(n). Hence O(2ⁿ · n) time, O(n) for the current subset.
approaches.explanation:
Maximising a count over a set screams 'try every subset'. Enumerate all 2ⁿ subsets, discard any with an overlapping pair, and remember the largest that survives.

**Why it's a valid starting point.** It's obviously correct — by checking every subset it cannot miss the optimum. It also makes the problem's structure explicit: we're choosing a subset, with a single feasibility constraint (pairwise non-overlap).

**Why it's hopeless at scale.** 2ⁿ explodes immediately — n = 40 is already a trillion subsets. The constraints allow n up to 10⁵, so exponential enumeration is a non-starter.

**Why greedy can replace it.** The key realisation is that we don't need to explore subsets at all. There's a single, locally-checkable rule — always extend by the earliest-finishing compatible activity — that provably reaches an optimum. The exchange argument (below) guarantees we never need to backtrack, collapsing 2ⁿ work into one sorted pass.
approaches.insight: Brute force shows the search space is exponential and the only constraint is pairwise compatibility. That single, simple constraint is exactly what lets a greedy rule succeed — when feasibility is local (just 'don't overlap the previous pick'), a globally optimal order usually exists.

python.line: ok = all(chosen[i][0] >= chosen[i - 1][1] for i in range(1, len(chosen)))
python.explanation: Valid only if consecutive (start-sorted) activities never overlap.

pitfalls: Trying to run this for n beyond ~25 — 2ⁿ is astronomically slow.
Checking overlap without sorting the subset first — you'd need all O(k²) pairs.
Confusing 'max count' with 'max total duration' — different objective.

approaches.name: Greedy by Earliest Finish Time (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with 'sort by finish time' and back it with the exchange argument.
hints: You want to keep as many activities as possible. Intuitively, which single activity should you commit to first so the most time is left for others?
The one that FINISHES earliest leaves the largest free tail. Sort by finish time and take the first activity; then repeatedly take the next activity that starts after your last finish.
Why is 'earliest finish' safe rather than just a heuristic? Try the exchange argument: swap any optimal solution's first activity for the earliest-finishing one and show nothing breaks.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting by finish time is O(n log n). The single scan that picks compatible activities is O(n). Only a counter and lastEnd are stored, so O(1) extra space beyond the sort.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the activities by finish time. Walk them in that order, keeping a running `lastEnd`. Take an activity whenever its start ≥ `lastEnd`, then set `lastEnd` to its finish. The number taken is the maximum possible.

**Why earliest finish, not earliest start or shortest duration.** Earliest *start* fails: a single activity that starts at time 0 but runs to time 100 would be picked first and block everything. Shortest *duration* fails too: a short activity sitting in the middle can straddle and knock out two others that could have coexisted. Earliest *finish* is the choice that frees up the most remaining timeline for subsequent activities — it's the least 'greedy with time'.

**The exchange argument (why greedy is optimal).** Let g be the activity with the globally earliest finish time, and let OPT be any optimal solution. Order OPT by finish time and call its first activity a. Because g finishes no later than a (g has the earliest finish of all), every activity in OPT that was compatible with a is also compatible with g — they all start at or after a's finish ≥ g's finish. So we can swap a out and g in, producing a new solution of the *same size* that is still valid and now contains g. By induction, after fixing g as the first pick, the remaining problem is the same kind of problem on the activities that start after g's finish, and the same swap applies. Therefore some optimal solution starts with the earliest-finishing activity — which is exactly what greedy picks — so greedy attains the optimum. Greedy never has to reconsider a choice: each pick is provably part of an optimal solution.

**Why a single pass suffices.** Once sorted by finish time, the only state we need is the finish time of the last activity we committed to. Any activity whose start clears that boundary is compatible with everything chosen so far (they all finished even earlier), so a linear scan with one comparison per activity is enough — no nested checks.
approaches.insight: Greedy works here because the feasibility test is purely local: an activity is compatible with the whole chosen set iff it's compatible with the most recently finished one. Sorting by finish time makes 'most recently finished' also the 'leaves the most room' choice, and the exchange argument certifies that this local rule yields the global optimum.

Compatible iff this start clears the last committed finish.
Advance the boundary to the finish of the activity just taken.

pitfalls: Sorting by start time or duration instead of finish time — both have counterexamples.
Comparing against the previous activity in input order rather than the last SELECTED finish.
Using `>` when the problem treats touching endpoints as compatible (or vice versa).
Sorting the start[] and finish[] arrays independently — that destroys the pairing; sort together.

edgeCases.behavior: Only the first is taken; the rest fail start ≥ lastEnd → count 1.
Every activity clears the previous finish → count n.

commonMistakes: Sorting by start time or shortest duration instead of finish time.
Comparing each activity to the previous one in order rather than to the last SELECTED finish.
Sorting start[] and finish[] separately, breaking the start-finish pairing.
Getting the boundary convention wrong (>= vs >) for touching endpoints.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting by start time instead of finish time
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An activity that starts first but runs very long gets picked and blocks everything after it. Sorting by finish time avoids this by always freeing the most future room.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to the previous activity, not the last selected
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you skip an overlapping activity, the reference must stay the last activity you actually took. Comparing to the immediately previous (possibly skipped) one lets overlaps slip through.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting the two arrays independently
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Sorting start[] and finish[] as separate arrays shuffles each independently and destroys which start goes with which finish, producing garbage intervals.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: activities = sorted(zip(start, finish), key=lambda a: a[1])

patternNote: Canonical sort-by-finish-time greedy for intervals. Whenever you maximise a count of non-overlapping intervals on a single resource, sort by end and take the earliest-finishing compatible one. The same engine powers Non-overlapping Intervals, Burst Balloons, and Pair Chain.
